(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- docs-consistency-guard: Documentation agent that audits docs for staleness and inconsistency AND generates/updates documentation on request. Use proactively when reviewing any PR that touches CLAUDE.md, docs/adr/, CONTRIBUTING.md, or docs/architecture.md. Also invoke when the user asks "is the documentation up to date?", "update the milestone", "scaffold the ADR for X", "add this to the ADR index", "add a TODO item", "scaffold a README for X", or "create a doc stub for Y." (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, Edit)

Audits whether the covering tests hand-build the value in the shape our model expects (the "fixture encodes our model" defect that hid (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. - pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- qa-verifier: QA/QE agent that (1) runs the full local verification battery mirroring CI's required checks before any commit/push/PR, (2) audits test quality on changed code — failure-mode coverage, mocked-seam smells, coverage on changed files (Week-8 ≥80% gate), and (3) exercises the running application with data-level scenarios — authoring suites/checks through the real API, negative and edge-case inputs, authz probes — against the local stack's seeded demo data. Use proactively before pushing a branch or opening a PR, after writing or modifying tests, or when the user asks "run the gate", "is this ready to push?", "is this tested enough?", or "smoke the app with bad data". - regression-mutation-verifier: Proves that a new regression test actually fails against the unfixed code. - ui-tester: End-to-end UI QA agent that exercises DataQ's frontend on BOTH desktop and mobile viewports (functionality + rendering) against the running app, AND audits backend↔frontend feature parity — flagging backend capabilities with no frontend surface (and frontend calls with no backend). ## claude.ai Microsoft Learn
# Microsoft Learn MCP Server

This server gives structured access to official Microsoft and Azure documentation via three tools:

## Tools

### microsoft_docs_search
Search official documentation and return up to 10 concise, high-quality content chunks (max 500 tokens each), including title, URL, and excerpt.

- Use first to get a quick, reliable overview
- Ideal for grounding answers in Microsoft knowledge

### microsoft_code_sample_search
Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn documentation and return up to 20 relevant, high-quality code samples.

- Use when you need to provide sample Microsoft/Azure related code in your answers.  
- Ideal for generating code snippets or practical implementation examples.  
- Optional parameter `language` can filter results. 

### microsoft_docs_fetch
Fetch and convert full Microsoft documentation pages to markdown.

- Use after search when you need full content from a specific URL
- Required for detailed tutorials, troubleshooting, prerequisites, code samples, or when search results are incomplete or outdated

## Workflow

1. Use `microsoft_docs_search` to find relevant documents.
2. If you need code examples or practical snippets, use `microsoft_code_sample_search`.
3. If deeper or complete information is needed, use `microsoft_docs_fetch`.

**Search gives breadth. Code Sample Search gives practical examples. Fetch gives depth.**

All content comes from Microsoft Learn or official sources, returned in clean markdown format.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". - loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). - schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. - run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). Here's what the search reveals about the ChainDrop npm supply chain attack:

## Overview

## ChainDrop Attack Overview

A self-propagating malware named 'ChainDrop' has compromised more than 1,300 packages with a combined 2 billion monthly downloads on the Node Package Manager (npm) registry. On August 4, 2026 (UTC), a self-propagating supply chain worm, which we are calling ChainDrop, ripped through npm.

## Highly Downloaded Packages Affected

Infected packages include very popular ones such as Keyv and Cacheable, flat-cache and file-entry-cache, all caching utilities from the same maintainer. In under four hours it poisoned 444 packages and 2,212 versions across more than a dozen victim organizations, including keyv@6.0.0 (over 150M weekly downloads), flat-cache@6.1.24 (149.9M), and file-entry-cache@11.1.6 (147.6M).

## Attack Origin and Spread

The supply-chain attack started after the threat actor compromised the GitHub account of Keyv's maintainer, and quickly spread to packages associated with major organizations such as Deliveroo, Ornikar, OneReach, Picsart, Qlik, and ServiceTitan.

## Technical Details

The tarball adds obfuscated loader files (observed as setup.mjs and math_init.js) and wires them into the package's preinstall lifecycle hook, so the code runs during dependency resolution rather than at import time. Merely installing or restoring the dependency tree is enough to execute it; the package never has to be required by application code.

For a comprehensive list of affected packages, you may want to check StepSecurity's OSS Security Feed or Aikido's reports, which are tracking the ongoing incident.

content.content:
# ChainDrop npm Worm: Critical Supply Chain Attack Summary

## Affected Packages & Versions

**Primary worm carriers (11 packages):**
- `keyv@6.0.0` (153.7M weekly downloads)
- `flat-cache@6.1.24` (149.9M)
- `file-entry-cache@11.1.6` (147.6M)
- `cacheable@2.5.1`, `cacheable-request@13.0.20`, `cache-manager@7.2.10`
- `@cacheable/utils@2.5.1`, `@cacheable/memory@2.2.1`, `@cacheable/node-cache@3.1.2`, `@cacheable/net@2.1.1`
- `ecto@5.0.1`

**Secondary wave:** 433 additional packages with 2,201 malicious versions total, republished via stolen credentials across `@servicetitan`, `@onereach`, `@qlik`, `@picsart`, `@deliveroo`, and others.

## Timeline & Attack Window

**First malicious publication:** August 4, 2026, 09:35 UTC (keyv@6.0.0)  
**Exposure window:** Roughly 1-2 hours initially; malicious versions remained as `latest` for several hours afterward

## Malware Capabilities

**Payload characteristics:**
- Two-stage attack: `setup.mjs` dropper (30KB, obfuscated) downloads official Bun runtime
- `Math_Symbol.js` stage 2 (728KB) executes with full credential harvesting
- Runs via `"preinstall": "node setup.mjs"` hook during npm install

**What it steals:**
- GitHub and npm tokens; AWS, Kubernetes, Vault credentials
- GitHub Actions runner memory scraping (targets `"isSecret":true` JSON fragments)
- AI tool credentials (`.claude/`, `.cursor/`, `.openai/`, `.anthropic/`)
- Cloud secrets across 16+ AWS regions via STS, Secrets Manager, SSM

**Propagation & persistence:**
- Re-publishes infected packages using harvested maintainer tokens
- Plants `.claude/` and `.vscode/` hooks for AI agent reinfection
- Installs token monitor (`gh-token-monitor.sh`) that triggers on credential revocation
- Ethereum blockchain C2 resolution (contract `0xE1f2395ee43e45A1556EC6438a88c31B83493103`)
- Exfiltration domain observed: `npm-cache.com`

## Key IOCs

**File artifacts:**
- `setup.mjs` (SHA-256: 54dc7ea5... or fd3ca400...)
- `Math_Symbol.js`/`math_init.js` (SHA-256: 9fc2570b...)
- `$TMPDIR/bun-dl-*` staging directories
- `.claude/setup.mjs`, `.vscode/tasks.json` persistence files

**Network indicators:**
- Ethereum RPC calls to resolve C2 domains
- `npm-cache.com:443/router` exfiltration endpoint
- Unexpected `github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download` during install steps

## Immediate Remediation

1. **Search lockfiles** for exact version matches; assume any system that installed these is compromised
2. **Rotate all credentials:** npm tokens, GitHub PATs, cloud keys, SSH keys, Kubernetes tokens
3. **Downgrade safely:** `npm install keyv@5.6.0 flat-cache@6.1.23 file-entry-cache@11.1.5 --ignore-scripts`
4. **Remove token monitor** before rotating GitHub tokens (prevents persistence trigger)
5. **Audit for persistence:** Check for `.claude/` and `.vscode/` config injections across repositories and developer machines

## Detection & Prevention

- Run `npm install --ignore-scripts` to prevent preinstall execution
- Implement 3-7 day minimum release age policies on new packages
- Enforce egress allowlists blocking `npm-cache.com` and Ethereum RPC endpoints
- Monitor for unsigned commits to release branches and unexpected GitHub Releases

content.text:
## Verdict: not impacted

ChainDrop is real and it's breaking right now — first malicious publish was **today, 2026-08-04 09:35 UTC** (`keyv@6.0.0`), a Shai-Hulud–derived worm that has hit 1,300+ packages. We are clean, but not by luck — worth reading why, because one of the mitigations is fragile.

**We do carry all three headline packages** — they arrive transitively under ESLint — but at versions the worm never touched:

| Package | Ours (in tree) | Malicious | Reachable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `keyv` | 4.5.4 | 6.0.0 | No |
| `flat-cache` | 4.0.1 | 6.1.24 | No |
| `file-entry-cache` | 8.0.0 | 11.1.6 | No |

Evidence, in order of strength:

1. **Semver-locked out, not just lagging.** [eslint/package.json:132](frontend/node_modules/eslint/package.json#L132) pins `"file-entry-cache": "^8.0.0"` — a caret on 8 cannot resolve to 11.1.6, and the rest of the chain (`file-entry-cache@8 → flat-cache@4 → keyv@4.5.4`) follows from that. Even an unpinned reinstall today lands on the same versions.
2. **Lockfile predates the attack by 8 days** — [frontend/pnpm-lock.yaml](frontend/pnpm-lock.yaml) last moved `2cf4f791` (2026-07-27), and git reports it unmodified.
3. **CI can't drift.** All three install steps in [ci.yml](.github/workflows/ci.yml#L273) use `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`. The one `npm install` (line 511) is `semver@7.8.5`, exact-pinned and dependency-free.
4. **No secondary-wave scopes** — zero lockfile hits for `@servicetitan`, `@onereach`, `@qlik`, `@picsart`, `@deliveroo`, `ornikar`, `cacheable*`, `cache-manager`, `ecto`.
5. **No IOCs on disk** — no `setup.mjs`, `Math_Symbol.js`, `math_init.js`, or `gh-token-monitor.sh` anywhere in the repo or installed tree; no `preinstall` hook in any installed package; no `bun-dl-*` staging dirs; no `npm-cache.com` in shell history or `/etc/hosts`; `.claude/` and `.vscode/` carry no injected files (this strain specifically plants `.claude/setup.mjs` and `.vscode/tasks.json` to re-infect AI agents, so I checked those explicitly).
6. **The `npx -y` MCP servers in [.mcp.json](.mcp.json) are clean** — the real floating surface, since they resolve fresh at every launch with no lockfile. Neither was republished in the attack window (`@upstash/context7-mcp` latest 2026-07-25, `@azure/mcp` latest 2026-07-31), and their dep trees are `zod`/`undici`/`express`/`commander`/MCP-SDK plus platform binaries — none affected.

**One negative I won't count:** my scan of `~/.npm/_cacache` returned nothing, but the positive control also returned nothing, so that scan was inconclusive rather than clean. The pnpm store is authoritative and it's clean, so the conclusion holds — but I'm not claiming the npm cache as evidence.

**No credential rotation needed.** Rotation is warranted only on evidence of execution, and there is none.

## The one real exposure

Our protection is a caret range, and **Dependabot is enabled for npm** (CLAUDE.md §6). An ESLint major bump is exactly the event that would move `file-entry-cache` from `^8` into the `11.x` line — and Dependabot opens those automatically. `pnpm audit --audit-level=high` is a merge gate, but advisory data for a hours-old worm lags.

I'd suggest, in priority order:
1. **Hold all npm Dependabot merges for ~7 days** and apply a minimum-release-age policy — the standard mitigation for this class.
2. Add `--ignore-scripts` where feasible; the payload runs from `preinstall`, so it fires on install alone, never needing to be imported.
3. Consider pinning `@upstash/context7-mcp` to an exact version like the `@azure/mcp` entry already is — CLAUDE.md's "pin majors" rule leaves `@1` free to float on every launch.

Want me to file a hardening issue for those three and open the PR for the release-age policy?

Sources: [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/massive-chaindrop-npm-supply-chain-attack-infects-hundreds-of-packages/) · [StepSecurity IOC writeup](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/chaindrop-npm-worm) · [Semgrep](https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/its-not-npm-ver-yet-npm-worm-chaindrop-hits-400-packages-including-jaredwray-servicetitan-ornikar-qlik-and-nebulajs/)

The allowlist treats a **stale entry as a hard `exit 2`**, so CI demands each waiver's deletion once the dependency moves on — that is what makes #968/#969 self-closing instead of forgotten.

Two things only checking could have told me, both recorded because guessing would have gone the other way: forcing brace-expansion 5 everywhere **breaks lint outright** (`minimatch@3` declares `^1.1.7` and calls the default export v5 dropped — `TypeError: expand is not a function`), and monaco's 0.56 worker file **still exists**; only the path to reach it changed. Both new allowlist guards were **mutation-checked** before being trusted.

**CodeQL: 6 open → 0.** Only one was a real finding (#56, `py/unnecessary-lambda` in a test — fixed in [#972](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/972)). The other five were dismissed with reasons recorded on each alert: #52/#53/#57/#58 (`py/cyclic-import` in `lineage/`) are the **deliberate** lazy-import registry in `warehouse.py:170-184` — no cycle exists at import time; #61 (`COMPARISON_KIND` unused) is a false positive, the constant is used across 8 modules and the query only sees module-local reads.

And the repo's technical claims were taken at face value; no PoC was run. Neither changes the verdict, since non-intersection holds whether or not the bugs are real.

### Upstream supply-chain triage — `ChainDrop` npm worm (2026-08-04)

Triaged the **ChainDrop** npm worm — a self-propagating Shai-Hulud derivative, first malicious publish `keyv@6.0.0` at **2026-08-04 09:35 UTC** (i.e. same-day), 1,300+ packages and ~2B monthly downloads, spreading by harvesting npm/GitHub tokens from install-time environments and re-publishing with them. **Verdict: not impacted — no code change warranted.** Recorded because this one is *unlike* the `bikini` triage above: all three headline packages **are** in our graph, so "not impacted" is a **version** claim, not an absence claim — and the thing holding it is a caret range.

| Package | Ours (lockfile + installed) | Malicious | Why it misses |
|---|---|---|---|
| `keyv` | 4.5.4 | 6.0.0 | Two majors below; arrives only under `flat-cache@4` |
| `flat-cache` | 4.0.1 | 6.1.24 | Two majors below; arrives only under `file-entry-cache@8` |
| `file-entry-cache` | 8.0.0 | 11.1.6 | `eslint@9` declares `"file-entry-cache": "^8.0.0"` — a caret on 8 **cannot** resolve to 11.x |

All three are transitive under ESLint; none is a declared dependency in `frontend/package.json`. The chain is `eslint@9 → file-entry-cache@8 → flat-cache@4 → keyv@4.5.4`, so the caret at the top pins the whole chain — **even an unpinned reinstall today lands on the same versions**. That is the real reason we are safe; the rest is corroboration: the lockfile last moved `2cf4f791` (2026-07-27, eight days before the attack) and is unmodified; all three frontend installs in `ci.yml` are `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (the one `npm install`, line 511, is exact-pinned dependency-free `semver@7.8.5`); and the lockfile has zero hits for the secondary-wave scopes (`@servicetitan`, `@onereach`, `@qlik`, `@picsart`, `@deliveroo`, `ornikar`, `cacheable*`, `cache-manager`, `ecto`).

**IOC sweep clean.** No `setup.mjs` / `Math_Symbol.js` / `math_init.js` / `gh-token-monitor.sh` in the repo or installed tree, no `preinstall` hook in any installed package (the payload fires from `preinstall`, so installation alone is enough — it never has to be imported), no `bun-dl-*` staging dirs, no `npm-cache.com` in shell history or `/etc/hosts`. Checked explicitly because **this strain targets AI-agent configs for re-infection**: it plants `.claude/setup.mjs` and `.vscode/tasks.json`, and harvests `.claude/` / `.cursor/` / `.anthropic/` credentials. Both directories are clean, here and in `$HOME`.

The `npx -y` MCP servers in `.mcp.json` were checked separately, since they are the one surface with **no lockfile** — they re-resolve at every launch. Both are clean: neither was republished in the attack window (`@upstash/context7-mcp` latest 2026-07-25, `@azure/mcp` latest 2026-07-31), and their dependency sets (`zod`, `undici`, `express`, `commander`, MCP SDK, platform binaries) do not include any affected package.

**No credential rotation performed, deliberately** — rotation is warranted on evidence of *execution*, and there is none. Worth stating because the standard incident advice is "rotate everything"; applying it without an execution signal would have meant re-minting the Key Vault `conn-*` set, and per the live-connections note one credential is N per-connection secrets that must each be re-tested or some silently stay dead.

**Two caveats kept deliberately.** (1) My `~/.npm/_cacache` scan returned nothing, **but so did the positive control** — that scan was *inconclusive*, not clean, and is not counted as evidence; the pnpm store is authoritative and it is clean. Recorded because an empty result from a scan that cannot hit anything reads identically to a real all-clear. (2) The protection is a **caret range, not a pin** — an ESLint major bump is exactly what would move `file-entry-cache` from `^8` into the `11.x` line, and Dependabot opens those automatically for npm. `pnpm audit --audit-level=high` is a merge gate, but advisory data for a hours-old worm lags it. Hardening (minimum-release-age policy, `--ignore-scripts`, pinning `@upstash/context7-mcp` to an exact version the way `@azure/mcp` already is) was **considered and consciously not taken** in this pass.

### Pending design decisions

The case that actually happens is the FIRST `/me` being throttled, where there is no cached answer to hold and the fix is to stay loading and retry — a different shape from the issue's sketch. **Writing the test is what exposed it**, which is the session's recurring lesson arriving from the other direction: not a test that proves nothing, but a test that refuses to be written because the behaviour isn't there.) (**2026-07-26 (later) — LIVE TESTING against the fresh prod deploy found a real defect that three green suites could not.** A non-interactive bearer (`az account get-access-token` on the api scope, #565) against `/api/v1/connections` showed **both Airflow connections at 282 and 280 consecutive poll failures** — ~47 hours broken. **That diagnosis was WRONG and is corrected on the issue** — I read the 404 and the `/api/v1/` URL shape and concluded Airflow 3 had moved the API to `/api/v2/`, without checking whether the host was up. It is not: `dataq-harness-airflow` is **`Stopped`**, deliberately, per the 2026-07-04 cost wind-down (#590), and ACA's ingress serves its unavailable page with a 404. `/api/v2/version` returns the same Azure error page, which would have said so immediately. [#1023](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1023) is rescoped to what survives: the classified reason tells the operator to check a connection config that is fine, when the signal is really that the host is unreachable — and a deliberately-offline integration now accumulates unbounded failures AND alerts (#842/#843), which wants a decision rather than a default. **The lesson is the one already written down and not applied: verify the reason, not just the result** — a green-looking inference from a status code is still an inference. Two things worth keeping: **#828's health counter is what made it findable at all** — that fact used to live only in logs — and **the classified reason points the wrong way**, telling the operator to 'check the connection and the suite's run target' when nothing is wrong with either; a 404 from a KNOWN provider endpoint is a version-compatibility signal, not a user misconfiguration. Also filed [#1024](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1024): `credential_expires_at` is NULL on all 13 prod connections including the two SAS-bearing ADLS ones, because #838 computes on secret write plus a DAILY sweep — so on a fresh deploy the feature delivers nothing for the existing estate for up to 24h, and NULL now means both 'no readable expiry' and 'not looked yet', which the UI cannot distinguish. **Neither would have surfaced from any test: one needed a live provider at its real version, the other needed a deploy with pre-existing rows.**) (**2026-07-26 (later still) — #788 CLOSED**, the last AC landing in the shape that actually occurs rather than the one sketched. The per-IP unauth bucket is shared across endpoints, so a burst anywhere can 429 `/me` — and painting PageError for it is wrong twice over: the app is fine, and the answer arrives on its own seconds later, meanwhile a workspace admin has lost the Admin and Settings nav. `MeProvider` now stays in `loading` and retries when the server said to; a spinner is the honest state where an error page asserts something false. Bounded at three retries, because **an endless spinner is the one outcome worse than an error page** — indistinguishable from a hung app, with nothing to act on. Non-429 failures are untouched (a 500/403 is not self-healing and must reach PageError with its HTTP facts, #910/#930). The mutation check earned its keep twice: it confirmed all three retry tests are load-bearing, AND it exposed a leak in those tests — `vi.useRealTimers()` sat at the end of each test BODY, which a failing test never reaches, so fake timers bled into the next test and it timed out for a reason unrelated to its assertion. Three real failures plus one phantom; moved to `afterEach`. **Batch 5 now stands at #976 and #788 done, #936 and #925 open.**) (**2026-07-26 (end of day) — ops log + hook, and HARNESS_TODO retired.** Two incidents this week shared one shape: state that mattered lived only outside git, so nobody could tell a deliberate action from a fault. New [docs/ops-log.md](ops-log.md) records harness start/stop and credential rotation — the latter listing EVERY Key Vault secret written per rotation, the countermeasure to the partial rotation that left two Snowflake connections dead for three weeks. Git-tracked deliberately rather than harness-side: history is the point, and an untracked file has none. A `PostToolUse:Bash` hook keeps it current; **it took three attempts and every failure was the same mistake** — it fired on its own commit message (grepped the whole string), then still fired after anchoring (prose WORD-WRAPS, so a line began `harness_window.sh.`), and finally needed a whitespace-or-end boundary, because a real invocation is followed by arguments or nothing, never a full stop. Prod had exactly that after this morning's deploy, including the SAS-bearing connections whose expiry is printed in the token. Now dispatched from `beat_init` beside the existing gap recovery (one beat process per deployment → once per restart, not once per worker). The two startup tasks became a list with **independently guarded** dispatch — a single `try` around the loop would let the first broker hiccup silently drop every later task, and that failure looks identical to success because dispatch is fire-and-forget. Mutation-verified both ways. **#1024 stays OPEN for its second half**: NULL still conflates 'no readable expiry' (a Snowflake PAT — correctly unknowable) with 'not computed yet'; this shrinks the ambiguity window from a day to seconds without removing it.) A freshness monitor aimed at a declared-PII column echoed its value straight past the redaction machinery built for exactly that. It also made the marker's own rule false, which is how a rule erodes. **Built at the READ layer, not by threading a policy into `datasources/`** — my first scoping said the latter; reading `redact_sample_failures` showed the product already stores samples raw and masks at the read boundaries, so threading a policy down would have inverted that dependency to fix a redaction bug. (**2026-07-26 — TIER 2 (connection health) DONE: #998, #1024, #748, #999, #996.** Sequenced by dependency, and the order mattered every time. **#998** replaced the connection-wide failure count with per-suite streaks rolled up — a broken hourly suite used to fill the shared 20-run window and badge a connection whose credential was fine, telling the operator to re-auth something that worked; a connection is now degraded only when EVERY suite is failing, with the MINIMUM streak as the number (the strongest claim true of all of them). **#1024** gave NULL expiry one meaning via `credential_expiry_checked_at` — stamped on every read, so 'no readable expiry' stops being indistinguishable from 'never looked', which is what made an unchecked credential look safe. **#748** added `/readyz` (a real DB read, 2s-bounded) because during the 2026-07-10 lock incident `/healthz` stayed GREEN through 25 minutes of total read degradation; `/healthz` stays liveness-only on purpose, since a liveness probe that fails on a DB blip gets the container killed. **#999** is the one where measuring changed the answer: the planned index ALONE only halves a cost that stays linear in history (8.4→32.7→195.4ms at 1k/4k/16k runs per suite; with index 5.5→23.0→94.8ms). LATERAL alone is also linear. Only **both** are flat — **0.2ms at every size** — because the index lets Postgres stop after 20 entries per suite. AC 3 said 'measured, not assumed' and it was right to. **#996** then fired the alert edges off the run streak, reusing #843's delivery-driven logic rather than a second copy. **Three guards caught things I would have shipped:** two alembic revision-id COLLISIONS (I verified the id for one migration then hand-picked the next), the #990 model-vs-migration parity test catching the new index undeclared, and the #787 assert-side-effect guard catching my own test. **And a mutation survived that mattered** — deleting #996's hook from `run_suite` broke nothing, so the alerting could have shipped connected to nothing. Third instance this session of a safeguard that looks wired up and isn't, after the dead mock in #976 and the unwired redaction sink in #989.) Deleted rather than gated, because being a forgotten sibling is precisely how it escaped #989's redaction sweep two PRs earlier, and pinned as a 404 so it cannot creep back. **#727** moved target-shape resolution into `datasources/registry.py`, ending a second dispatch-by-type site that silently falsified the 'adding a datasource is one registry entry' contract (#716 already had to edit both) — now enforced by a test comparing the adapter set against the resolver set, not by a comment asking people to remember. **#905 closed by triage, not by building:** item 1 (beat liveness) shipped in #904 and was verified live today; item 2's stated goal — a wedged reconnect dies rather than hanging — is **met by item 1**, cause-agnostically, which is the property the issue itself argued for. I deliberately did NOT pin broker settings on top: the issue asks to *investigate* why the reconnect loop neither retried nor raised, I cannot establish that without reproducing the wedge, and shipping unverified settings against live prod is a placebo. Item 3 became [#1052](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1052) — workspace-wide `last_polled_at` staleness, the one signal that cannot lie, because every incident in this class is the worker looking alive and writing nothing, so anything derived from its own writes cannot fire when it is what broke. **Harness credentials fixed for #1032:** ACCOUNTADMIN PAT → the terraform provider (it creates account roles; `DATAQ_LOADER` cannot create itself), loader PAT → the KV secret the containers read; both verified by asserting `CURRENT_ROLE()`, not by the write succeeding. The targeted apply propagated it — **5 of the plan's 8 changes**, because a blanket apply would have ARMED both ADF triggers (`activated false -> true`) on a harness meant to be asleep, and silently altered the warehouse via provider drift. **The entry** — [docs/progress.md:124](docs/progress.md#L124), `### Upstream supply-chain triage — ChainDrop npm worm (2026-08-04)`, placed right after the `bikini/exploitarium` note and mirroring its shape: verdict up front, a table of the intersection, the corroborating evidence, then "two caveats kept deliberately."

So the verdict is a *version* claim, and what actually holds it is `eslint@9`'s `"file-entry-cache": "^8.0.0"` — a caret on 8 can't reach the malicious 11.1.6, which is why even an unpinned reinstall today is safe. The lockfile predating the attack and CI's `--frozen-lockfile` are corroboration, not the reason.

docs: progress — ChainDrop npm worm triage (not impacted) + Open-PRs row re-count

Records the 2026-08-04 triage of the ChainDrop npm supply-chain worm
(self-propagating Shai-Hulud derivative; first malicious publish
keyv@6.0.0 at 09:35 UTC; 1,300+ packages, ~2B monthly downloads).

Verdict: not impacted — no code change warranted.

Recorded because this is a different shape from the bikini/exploitarium
triage above it: all three headline packages ARE in our graph (keyv
4.5.4, flat-cache 4.0.1, file-entry-cache 8.0.0, transitively under
ESLint), so "not impacted" is a VERSION claim, not an absence claim.
What actually holds it is eslint@9's "file-entry-cache": "^8.0.0" — a
caret on 8 cannot resolve to the malicious 11.1.6, so even an unpinned
reinstall today lands on the same versions. The lockfile predating the
attack by 8 days and CI's --frozen-lockfile are corroboration, not the
reason.

Also captured: the IOC sweep (clean, incl. the .claude/ and .vscode/
AI-agent persistence paths this strain specifically targets), the
no-lockfile npx MCP surface in .mcp.json (clean; neither server
republished in the attack window), and the deliberate decision NOT to
rotate credentials — rotation is warranted on evidence of execution,
and there is none.

Two caveats kept deliberately:
- The ~/.npm/_cacache scan was INCONCLUSIVE, not clean — the positive
  control also returned nothing, so it is not counted as evidence. An
  empty result from a scan that could not hit anything reads exactly
  like a real all-clear.
- The protection is a caret range, not a pin. The next ESLint major is
  the event to re-check this note against. Hardening (minimum
  release-age, --ignore-scripts, pinning @upstash/context7-mcp exactly)
  was considered and consciously not taken.

Snapshot drift fixed in the same pass: the Open-PRs row read 0 while
GitHub had 12 (all Dependabot, opened 2026-08-03, none merged). Counted
live with `gh pr list --state open`, not by memory. That drift was
load-bearing for the note — 5 of the 12 are npm PRs open across the worm
window, so each was diff-checked rather than assumed: all five touch
pnpm-lock.yaml, none contains a line touching the keyv / flat-cache /
file-entry-cache / cacheable chain, and none bumps eslint.

Docs-only. No code, schema, or dependency change.

## Summary

- Records the **2026-08-04 triage of the ChainDrop npm supply-chain worm** against DataQ's dependency graph. **Verdict: not impacted — no code change warranted.** Written up in `docs/progress.md` alongside the existing `bikini/exploitarium` 0-day triage it deliberately contrasts with.
- **Why it's worth recording:** unlike the bikini triage (which rested on non-intersection), all three headline packages **are** in our graph — `keyv` 4.5.4, `flat-cache` 4.0.1, `file-entry-cache` 8.0.0, transitively under ESLint. So "not impacted" is a **version** claim, not an absence claim, and the thing holding it is a caret range: `eslint@9` declares `"file-entry-cache": "^8.0.0"`, which cannot resolve to the malicious `11.1.6`. Even an unpinned reinstall today lands on the same versions. That is the actual reason; the lockfile predating the attack by 8 days and CI's `--frozen-lockfile` are corroboration.
- **Fixes Snapshot drift found in the same pass:** the Open-PRs row read **0** while GitHub had **12** (all Dependabot, opened 2026-08-03, none merged). Re-counted live with `gh pr list --state open`, not from memory.

## Linked issue

None — no defect, no issue filed. The triage concluded *not impacted*, and the hardening options were consciously declined (recorded in the note itself so it reads as a decision, not an oversight).

## Type of change

- [ ] feat — new functionality
- [ ] fix — bug fix (linked issue above)
- [ ] chore — repo housekeeping / tooling
- [x] docs — documentation only
- [ ] refactor — no behaviour change
- [ ] test — test-only change

- [x] **Manually tested locally** (see notes below — the triage itself is the testing)
- [x] **Single functionality** — one triage note + the Snapshot row it depends on
- [x] **Conventional commit title** (`docs:`)
- [x] **No secrets, credentials, or `.env` files committed**
- [x] **Black + Ruff + mypy pass locally** — N/A (no Python); `pre-commit run --files docs/progress.md` passed incl. betterleaks secret scan
- [x] **Prettier + ESLint pass locally** — N/A (no frontend source change)
- [ ] **Tests added/updated** — N/A, docs-only
- [x] **Docs / ADRs updated** — this PR *is* the doc update
- [ ] **`docs/progress.md` updated** — flip roadmap task(s)
- [x] **`docs/progress.md` — N/A** for this PR (pure docs; no roadmap task maps to it)
- [x] **Security implications considered** — see risk notes

## Schema migration?

- [x] No schema change
- [ ] Yes — Alembic migration included

## Manual test notes

The triage is the verification. What was actually run:

- **Lockfile + installed tree** — `keyv@4.5.4`, `flat-cache@4.0.1`, `file-entry-cache@8.0.0` confirmed in both `frontend/pnpm-lock.yaml` and `node_modules/.pnpm/`; malicious versions are `6.0.0` / `6.1.24` / `11.1.6`.
- **Semver reachability** — `frontend/node_modules/eslint/package.json:132` declares `"file-entry-cache": "^8.0.0"`; chain is `eslint@9 → file-entry-cache@8 → flat-cache@4 → keyv@4.5.4`.
- **Secondary wave** — zero lockfile hits for `@servicetitan`, `@onereach`, `@qlik`, `@picsart`, `@deliveroo`, `ornikar`, `cacheable*`, `cache-manager`, `ecto`.
- **CI drift** — all three frontend installs in `ci.yml` are `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`; the one `npm install` (line 511) is exact-pinned, dependency-free `semver@7.8.5`.
- **IOC sweep** — no `setup.mjs` / `Math_Symbol.js` / `math_init.js` / `gh-token-monitor.sh`, no `preinstall` hook in any installed package, no `bun-dl-*` staging dirs, no `npm-cache.com` in shell history or `/etc/hosts`. `.claude/` and `.vscode/` checked explicitly (here and in `$HOME`) because this strain plants `.claude/setup.mjs` + `.vscode/tasks.json` to re-infect AI agents.
- **npx MCP surface** — the `.mcp.json` servers re-resolve at every launch with no lockfile; neither was republished in the attack window (`@upstash/context7-mcp` latest 2026-07-25, `@azure/mcp` latest 2026-07-31) and their dep sets contain no affected package.
- **The 5 open npm Dependabot PRs** (#1168/#1172/#1173/#1175/#1176) were each diff-checked rather than assumed: all touch `pnpm-lock.yaml`, none contains a line touching the affected chain, none bumps `eslint`.
- **Anchor + counts** — heading slug verified against the in-doc link; issue counts re-verified live (25 in `v1.1 Backlog` / 42 repo-wide — unchanged, so left alone).

## Security / risk notes

- **No credential rotation was performed, deliberately.** Rotation is warranted on evidence of *execution*, and there is none. Stated explicitly in the note because the reflexive incident response is "rotate everything" — doing that without an execution signal would mean re-minting the Key Vault `conn-*` set, where one credential is N per-connection secrets that must each be re-tested or some silently stay dead.
- **One negative is explicitly NOT counted as evidence:** the `~/.npm/_cacache` scan returned nothing, but so did the positive control, making it *inconclusive* rather than clean. The pnpm store is authoritative and is clean. Recorded because an empty result from a scan that could not have hit anything reads identically to a real all-clear.
- **Known-fragile mitigation, named as such:** the protection is a caret range, not a pin, and Dependabot opens npm majors automatically. The note names the next ESLint major as the event to re-check it against. Hardening (minimum release-age policy, `--ignore-scripts`, pinning `@upstash/context7-mcp` to an exact version the way `@azure/mcp` already is) was considered and consciously not taken in this pass.

content.text:
Committed and pushed — but the merge is blocked by something that isn't mine, and I found a second issue on the way.

**PR [#1177](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1177)** — branch `docs/chaindrop-supply-chain-triage`, commit `50454900`, milestone `v1.1 Week 6`, template filled. `main` is protected, so this is the PR route rather than a direct push. 21 insertions, `docs/progress.md` only.

## CI is red — pre-existing, not from this PR

`Frontend — dependency audit (pnpm audit)` fails; everything else passes (Bandit, both CodeQL, betterleaks, lint, type check, build). **It is not caused by this change** — `git diff main --stat` is `docs/progress.md` alone, so the lockfile my branch audits is byte-identical to `main`'s. I reproduced it locally with the real CI command (`node scripts/audit_bulk.cjs --audit-level=high` from `frontend/`, exit 1). This is the same shape as the 2026-07-24 sweep the doc describes: a new advisory red-lines every open PR, including docs-only ones.

Three high+ advisories, and **all three have a fix available**:

| Advisory | Current | Patched |
|---|---|---|
| `brace-expansion` GHSA-rgw5-rvv9-x895 (bypasses the CVE-2026-14257 mitigation) | 1.1.16 | **1.1.18** |
| same, 5.x line | 5.0.8 | **5.0.9** |
| `undici` GHSA-4cwx-7wf7-3272 (cross-user info disclosure) | 7.28.0 | **7.29.0** |

Worth flagging specifically: this also makes the **#969 waiver's premise stale**. Its recorded rationale is *"the 1.x line ends at 1.1.16"* and that forcing v5 breaks lint because `minimatch@3` calls a dropped default export. But 1.1.17 and 1.1.18 now exist on the 1.x line, so the bump is available *without* the v5 break that forced the waiver. That waiver may now be removable rather than re-scoped — which is exactly the self-closing behaviour the allowlist's stale-entry `exit 2` was built for.

## Second finding: pre-commit hooks aren't installed

`.git/hooks/pre-commit` **does not exist** in this clone, so my commit went through without hooks running — silently. I ran them manually against the file afterwards and all passed, including the betterleaks secret scan, so nothing bad landed. But this is worse than a `--no-verify` because there's no signal at all; the repo's "don't commit past hooks" rule is currently unenforceable locally, and CI is the only net. Fix is `pre-commit install` — a one-line local env change, no repo change.

## Still running

The `docs-consistency-guard` audit of the new entry is in the background — it's verifying my factual claims (the `eslint@9` caret, lockfile versions, CI flags, the anchor slug) and judging whether this triage warrants a standing-decisions row like the bikini one did. I'll report what it finds when it lands.

Three things I can do next, none of which I've started: install the pre-commit hook, open a separate follow-up PR for the three bumps (one functionality, so not folded into the docs PR), or merge #1177 once the gate is green. Which do you want?
